history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Welcome, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you tell me a little about what brings you in and what areas of your life or relationships have been feeling most challenging lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep noticing how everyone promises to help and then just leaves the mess for me to clean up, like the time the manager said she'd cover the back aisle and I ended up staying late fixing the shelves they never touched. It feels like I'm the only one who actually notices the details, and when I point it out people get defensive or just ignore it, so I write it down anyway. I know I quit jobs fast when the mistakes pile up, but I can't stand watching others screw up the way I need things done, and it wears me out.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds really exhausting to feel like you're constantly the only one carrying the load and catching the details. How does this pattern of having to take over or feeling let down by others show up in your personal relationships outside of work?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep finding myself fixing things—like that crooked shelf that I spent hours straightening, or the promises people break and then try to apologize like it’s nothing. It’s frustrating because I’m the only one who actually follows through, and when someone finally slips up I just quit before they can expect me to clean up again. I know I end up pulling away, but I’m still angry that they keep letting me carry the load.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When people fail to follow through or let things slide like that, what goes through your mind about why they are doing it and what their intentions might be toward you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep catching them—like that manager who never posted the schedule and left me covering his shift—making promises they never keep and expecting me to clean up the mess. It feels like everyone’s just waiting for me to slip so they don’t have to take responsibility, so I end up holding all the pieces. I know I could walk away, but I can’t stand the thought of them getting away with half‑hearted work while I’m the one who notices every detail.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of work, what have your closest friendships or romantic relationships looked like over the years, and how easy or difficult has it been for you to truly trust someone?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about every time someone let me down—like the coworker who missed a shift I covered, the friend who forgot my birthday, the ex who vanished with the car keys—and I can’t shake the feeling that each of those moments proves I can’t trust anyone. It’s like I have this ledger in my head, cataloguing every broken promise, and the more I add to it, the harder it is to even consider letting anyone in. I know I’m supposed to move past it, but each new smile just feels like another chance for them to drop the tool I spent so long sharpening.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that ledger builds up and you feel so let down or angry, how do you typically handle those intense feelings in the moment, and have they ever led to impulsive reactions or heated confrontations?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When I see the ledger messed up again it feels like everyone around me is purposely screwing up, so I end up yelling at the clerk and then thinking about walking out, just like I did when they wouldn't give me those forms. I keep a mental note of every mistake, every time someone lies or tries to make me look bad, and I can’t stand the idea of just letting it slide. Sometimes I wonder if it even matters, because it seems like I'm the only one who fixes it while the others just watch and wait for me to explode. I could just quit, but I also want to have something to show them—a record of how they’ve failed me.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back, how far back in your life does this pattern of feeling like you can't trust others' intentions and needing to keep track of their mistakes go, even into your teenage years or earlier?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep noticing every little slip—like the manager who never gave the shift report or the coworker who skipped the inventory count—and it just adds up to proof that they’re hiding something. When the researchers refused to hand me the questionnaires I felt the same thing, like they were covering up the truth, so I write it down and move on. I can’t really trust anyone’s “sorry” or “it’s fine” because it always turns out to be another excuse. Sometimes I wonder why I even bother, but I just keep the record and walk away when it gets too much.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what kinds of challenges or recurring patterns in your life you've been hoping to explore?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spend most of my days moving the boxes around and trying to keep the shelves of my glow‑worm notes from collapsing, because that’s the only thing that still feels organized after my sister died. I told the landlord it was an emergency, not that she was gone, because I was terrified they'd throw us out and I couldn't even picture the apartment clean enough to stay. Sometimes I get tearful when I think about her, other times I just recite the facts about bioluminescence like a story, hoping some medical school will finally see the papers and maybe, in a way, give my work some meaning.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: I am so sorry for the loss of your sister. To help me understand how things have evolved, could you tell me what your daily life, relationships, and your research were like before she passed away?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I woke up this morning to the cracked blinds letting in a thin strip of light, the kettle whistling and the kitchen still warm from last night’s dishes, and I slipped my notebook—filled with sketches of glowing algae—under my arm as I headed down the hallway. I handed a few of those clippings to Mrs. Kowalski when she stopped by for sugar, trying not to draw the landlord’s eye, then sat on the worn couch and kept writing about skin that could shine with emotion, hoping someday a medical school might find something useful in my notes. At the same time, the empty apartment where my sister used to be feels heavier each day, and I keep moving the boxes around, not because I’m tidy, but because the familiar clutter somehow steadies me. Sometimes the thought of the landlord finally noticing the mess makes my chest tighten, yet I tell myself I’ll keep going, even if it feels like I’m talking to the walls more than to anyone else.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of the close bond you shared with your sister, what have your relationships and friendships with other people generally looked like throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spend most days just moving the same piles of papers around, trying to keep the apartment from looking like a disaster while I stare at my notes about glowing skin, and I tell myself it’s fine because at least the pages don’t ask me anything. The hallway is full of strangers who barely notice me, and the landlord’s stare makes me nervous about what might happen if he sees the mess, so I keep everything locked away and pretend I’m okay with being alone. Sometimes I think I’d smile if someone actually knocked and wanted to talk, but the silence in my flat feels safer than the possibility of being laughed at for my ideas.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned that silence feels safer than the risk of being laughed at for your ideas—has this worry about being criticized or judged by others been a long-standing pattern throughout your life, and how have people typically responded when you did try to open up?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I told the nurse about my glowing‑skin idea and she smiled, then went back to her chart, and I could feel that brief spark of excitement fade quickly into the same old quiet. My hands shake a little when I open the notebook, like the old pipes in the apartment, and I worry they’ll think I’m just an old man with odd papers. Still, I keep writing because the notes are the only thing that feels steady, even if everyone else just nods and moves on.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you work on these ideas about skin shining with emotion, is that something you have personally seen or physically experienced, or is it more of a theoretical project you have been developing?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about the idea of skin that glows when you feel something, and I imagine it like a little lamp in the dark, maybe it could finally make someone notice me. At the same time, I look at the piles of my notes on the kitchen table and wonder if it's just my imagination keeping me busy while the apartment stays messy and the landlord watches. I guess part of me wants a crowd to see that glow, but most days it feels like I'm just moving papers around, trying to hold onto something that still shines.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your adult life, how did you typically manage work, daily decisions, and caring for yourself before your sister passed away, and to what extent did you rely on her to help navigate those things?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going through the same little checklist in my head—turn off the lights, lock the door, water the plant—just like I used to do when she was around, and I still picture her bringing soup while I put the tools back in the box. The apartment feels empty now, and I find myself staring at my old bioluminescence notes, trying to keep that glow alive while the silence reminds me how much I relied on her reminders for even the simplest things. Sometimes I wonder if I ever managed anything on my own, but I just sit on the kitchen floor with a coffee and try to focus on the science instead of the emptiness.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of your home and your sister's care, what has your experience been with working, going to school, or making major life decisions independently throughout your adult life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been thinking about how the night classes and my notes on glowing skin have become the only things that feel steady, like the pipes I used to work on, and I keep rearranging the boxes in the apartment just enough so the landlord won’t notice the mess. I know I delayed reporting my sister’s death because I was scared of losing the place where I keep all those papers, not because I didn’t feel anything. It’s strange—sometimes I feel numb, other times I’m almost relieved that at least my research might outlive me, even if no one ever notices it now.

history.speaker: therapist

history.speaker: therapist

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep all of that stuff in my notebook because if I say anything people just stare at the drawings and call me weird. history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that pressure builds up like that, how does it affect you, and what do you typically do to cope when it feels like too much?

history.speaker: self

My mom keeps saying I’m “quiet,” the TA laughed at my drawings, and I can’t shake the feeling that everyone’s talking about me behind my back. Sometimes I just stare at the wall and imagine the ghosts taking the pressure away, but then that knot in my chest tightens and I don’t know if I should even be here.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel that knot tighten and wonder if you should even be here, what thoughts or urges come up for you, and have you ever done anything impulsive or harmful to try to cope with that distress?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like something's closing in on me, like the sketches I doodle when I’m alone, and I just want to lock the door and stay silent. I thought about flipping a coin to decide if I should even go to class today, but the idea of people looking at me makes the knot tighten even more. Maybe I’ll just sit in the dark, stare at the ceiling, and wait for the feeling to pass.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you stay in your room to get away from everyone, do you find yourself longing to have close friendships and feeling held back by fear of judgment, or do you genuinely feel more comfortable and content being completely on your own?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Sometimes the apartment feels like the walls are closing in, like the strange drawings in my notebook are staring back at me, and I keep wondering if flipping a coin would somehow tell me whether I should stay or just walk out. My mom always says I’m quiet and don’t have friends, and I can hear that in the silence, but the idea of someone actually knocking on my door makes me both nervous and oddly curious. I sit here and listen to the hum of the fridge, feeling like there’s something watching, even if there’s nothing there, and I can’t tell if that’s fear or just the emptiness that always follows when I shut the door.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, has there ever been anyone you felt you could completely trust and let your guard down around, or has it always felt necessary to keep your guard up with others?

history.speaker: self

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When someone criticizes your work or fails to recognize your skill the way you expect, how does that affect you emotionally, and what do you typically do in response?

history.speaker: self

It makes my blood boil, and I keep thinking about filing an ADA accommodation or even a lawsuit because they’re trying to make me look like a failure. history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When your blood boils like that, what does pushing back typically look like for you—have there been times where that anger led to physical altercations, impulsive decisions, or trouble with the law?

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To get us started, could you tell me a little about what brings you in and how things have generally been going in your day-to-day life and relationships?

history.text: You mentioned that you push people away even though a part of you wishes you weren't so alone—what typically goes through your mind or feels like it's happening when you start pulling back from someone who is trying to get close?

history.speaker: therapist

history.speaker: therapist

history.speaker: self

history.text: How far back in your life do these intense emotional shifts and relationship struggles go, and how have they affected your sense of who you are as a person?

My mother still looks at me like I’m some decent son, but I can’t shake the feeling that I’m just a joke they keep handing the bill to.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel that someone is looking down on you or acting with a hidden agenda, how do you typically respond or handle those situations?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I can tell they’re all watching me, thinking I’m just the guy who moved back in with my mother and is waiting for some free meal or a nice hotel night. It hurts, because I used to be the top broker, but now it feels like everyone’s just waiting for me to slip up so they can prove they’re better. I don’t need their pity or their applause, I’ll just keep my distance and do what I have to—maybe quit if it gets too much.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned sensing that people are constantly watching you and waiting for you to slip up. Could you give a specific example of what makes you feel that way, and share whether that kind of mistrust has been a common experience throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like everyone’s just waiting for me to mess up again—those residents, the car‑sales manager, even the receptionist at the lobby—they all have that look in their eyes, like they’re ready to pounce. I know I’m supposed to prove them wrong, but honestly, I’m tired of trying; it’s easier to just walk away and let Mom’s humming be the only thing that doesn’t feel like a judgment. Sometimes I wonder if I’m just being paranoid, but the sting of those moments still lingers, and I can’t shake the feeling that I’m still being watched.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life, even before working as a broker, have you always had this tendency to pull away when people felt judgmental or disappointing, or did that pattern start more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I just get the feeling everyone’s looking at me like I’m some arrogant loser who quit because the job was beneath me, so I shut down and stop trying to explain myself. When you…people with a nice smile try to help, I picture them just waiting for a free lunch, and it makes me want to roll my eyes and walk away. Still, I can’t shake that knot in my throat, like I’m choking on the embarrassment of living with my mom while pretending I’m fine in those fancy hotels.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—it's very good to meet you today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what has been going on in your life recently that brought you in to see me?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’m just trying to keep the smile on, even when I’m terrified of saying something stupid in class or worrying that my dad’s voice will pop up again. It’s easier when I’m outside with kids or a dog because they don’t seem to judge, they just appreciate what I do. At the same time, I keep telling myself I’m fine, even though inside I feel like I’m constantly waiting for the next thing to fall apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling terrified of being judged or saying something stupid, whereas you feel much more at ease around kids or pets who don't judge. When it comes to peers your own age, what typically happens when you try to interact or form closer relationships with them?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like I'm waiting for someone to call on me, heart racing, and I just smile and try to blend in, even though inside I'm terrified they'll notice I'm nervous. When I think about it, I hear my dad’s voice again, saying I’ll never be good enough, and I end up shrinking instead of speaking up. I wish I could be like the kids at the park—just be seen without all the judgment—so I end up pretending everything’s fine while the knot in my chest stays

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Deep down, do you find yourself wishing you had close, meaningful connections with peers if you knew you wouldn't be judged, or do you generally feel more comfortable keeping to yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking that if I could just speak without turning red, maybe people would actually see who I am, but every time I try I hear my dad’s voice saying I’m never enough, and I end up smiling and hiding the nervousness. I want to plan a real conversation with my mom, write down what I want to say, but the fear of messing up the list makes me freeze again. Even when I’m with the kids at the park, where nobody judges, a part of me still worries they’ll notice the shy girl who’s scared to let anyone in.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When those intense feelings of anxiety or fear of messing up become overwhelming, how do you typically cope with that distress—do you tend to strictly hold everything inside, or do you ever find yourself reacting in impulsive or intense ways?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like I’m going to mess up again, like that time in class when everyone stared and I just wanted to disappear, so I end up smiling and saying “I’m fine” even though my chest is tight. I know I could just tell someone what’s going on, but I’m scared they’ll think I’m too much, so I hide it and try to focus on the lab or the kids outside, hoping the wind will wash the panic away. Sometimes I wonder if I’ll ever be able to let anyone see the shaking without feeling like a failure.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you worry about how others are reacting to you, what do you typically believe their intentions or thoughts about you are in those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that everyone can see how nervous I am, like when I freeze in class and my cheeks turn pink, and I’m terrified they’ll think I’m just a fragile, “soft” person who can’t handle anything. At the same time, I try to smile and be the helpful cousin, hoping they won’t notice the doubt I feel inside, especially when I hear that old voice of my dad saying I never measure up. It’s like I’m stuck between wanting to disappear and wanting to be the good, obedient one, and I don’t know which part of me will win.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling that pull to be the "good, obedient one"—when it comes to making important decisions in your life, how comfortable are you relying on your own judgment versus needing reassurance or direction from others?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going over the schedule in my head, wondering if I’ll pick the wrong shift and everyone will notice, so I’m almost sure I’ll just end up asking my cousin again even though I’m scared he’ll roll his eyes. It feels like if I make a mistake it’ll prove what Dad always said—that I’m never good enough, and that thought just…sticks. At the same time, part of me wants to just trust my gut and do it on my own, but the fear of being judged makes me freeze. I don’t want to be the kid who never answered in class, but I also don’t want to feel that hollow emptiness again.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what has been going on in your life recently and what brought you in to talk?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been stuck in that endless inbox for two years, just doing what my boss says, and even now I feel like I’m reaching for the pills whenever the quiet gets too loud. I keep trying to be everything for everyone—going to operas I don’t enjoy, taking singing lessons just to keep a relationship alive—only to end up feeling hollow and ashamed when it falls apart. I want to be heard, to laugh, to make a decision on my own, but every time I think about stepping out I get shaky, panicky, and I’m not sure it’s even worth the effort.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry the weight of constantly reshaping yourself just to keep relationships afloat. When you think about showing someone who you truly are or facing the prospect of being on your own, what is the biggest fear that comes up for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that if I stop being the “yes‑person,” everyone will finally see how useless I am—my boss, the women I’ve dated, even myself. It feels like I’m just pretending to like things, like when I forced myself to enjoy opera for my ex, and now the silence feels louder than any argument. The pills make my hands shake when I think about doing anything on my own, and I don’t even know who I am without all those scripts.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When a relationship does come to an end and you're faced with that silence, how do you typically cope, and what does that period usually look like for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I just sit here and feel the silence get louder, like the office after the boss walks out, and I don’t know if I should fill it with some work or just… nothing. I keep thinking about calling her, but I’m scared I’ll sound clingy, so I stay quiet and let the emptiness swallow me, even though my hands start shaking and I can’t decide even what to eat. It’s like every time I try to do something, I end up waiting for someone else to tell me what’s right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life—whether with family, in school, or in previous jobs—has this difficulty making decisions and needing someone else to guide you been a constant pattern, or have there been times when you felt confident directing your own path?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking I could just choose a coffee for once, but then I get scared that I’ll pick the wrong one and everyone will notice, so I end up waiting for the boss to tell me what to get. It’s the same with everything else—like when I booked that opera ticket on my own, I felt a moment of pride, but then the anxiety rushed in and I wanted someone else to say I was doing okay. I know I’m supposed to be okay with it, but I still end up taking the pills, feeling the shake, and then the panic hits again, and I just want to hide and cry like after that breakup.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When an important relationship comes to an end, do you find yourself feeling an urgent need to quickly find someone new to rely on and guide you, or do you tend to withdraw and avoid getting close to people altogether?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself I should just stay quiet and let everything settle, but then I hear that little voice inside me that wants to call someone, to fill the emptiness before it gets too loud. I think about the opera nights, how I pretended to love that world just to keep her, and now it feels like another dead‑end hallway I’m stuck in. My hands are shaking, the pills are humming, and I’m scared that if I disappear the silence will just prove how useless I am, yet the thought of being alone scares me even more.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: In your close relationships, do things ever become stormy with sudden anger or intense emotional swings, or do you find that you almost always hold everything in and go along with whatever they want just to keep them close?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself it’s easier to just say yes, even when I don’t want to, because I’m terrified that if I say no they’ll just leave and I’ll be alone. It feels like I’m always fitting into whatever role someone else wants, whether it’s the boss’s orders or trying to impress a girlfriend, and I don’t even know what I’d ask for if I could. The quiet that comes after I finally say no feels like a hollow ringing, like I’ve disappeared, so I keep swallowing my own wishes just to keep the peace.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, welcome. I’m glad we could meet today, and I want to make sure this is a comfortable space for you to share what's on your mind. To help us get started, could you tell me a bit about what brought you in, and how things have generally been going in your daily life and relationships lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going over the inventory of his stuff, even the old headphones I promised to find a place for, because if something goes missing it feels like I’m losing a part of us. I stay up late to finish my to‑do list and wake before sunrise to straighten the shelves again, hoping the order will keep the anxiety at bay, even though I can see it pushing him away. At work they praise me, but I still find myself double‑checking everyone’s answers, asking “are you sure?” because I can’t tolerate a detail slipping through. I know I’m hard‑headed and it hurts, but I’m terrified of letting anything fall apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry the weight of keeping everything in place, especially when you feel it creating distance with your partner. When you feel that terror of things falling apart or a detail slipping through, what is the deepest fear or outcome that feels like it's looming in those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking that if something falls off a shelf or a box gets misplaced, it’s not just a mess—it feels like I’ve failed him and everything else I’ve worked so hard to keep together. I’m terrified that a tiny slip, like missing a checkbox on a case, will expose all the cracks I’ve been hiding behind the order, and then I’ll be left with an empty room and no way to hold onto anything. I know I’m being rigid, but I can’t shake the feeling that without that structure everything just unravels.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned hiding "cracks" behind all of this order—when you picture those cracks being exposed, what do you worry people would see about who you are, and has that feeling of needing to hold everything together been with you throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going over the shelves in my head, making sure every box is where I said it would be, because if I leave even one thing out it feels like I'm slipping, like I'm losing control of the whole place. My boyfriend asked me to get rid of that old lamp, and I just said we could talk about it later, but inside I’m terrified that if I actually toss something, the whole room will start falling apart. I’m exhausted, but I still wake up early to label everything again, just to prove to myself that I can still hold it together even when the walls are cracking.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When your boyfriend presses you to let something like the lamp go, or when someone disrupts the order you've set up, what happens to your emotions and how do you tend to handle it between the two of you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When he says we should toss something, I get this surge of panic, like the whole order I’ve built is about to collapse, so I can’t help but argue to keep it. I know I’m being rigid, but if I let go of even one little thing I worry it’ll be something important that I’ll regret losing later. That same tension follows me at work—when a file is out of place I feel compelled to reorganize it, even if it means staying up past nine and looking like a micromanager. I guess I’m scared that if I don’t keep everything perfect, everything will just fall apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of these struggles with order and control, how do your moods and relationships tend to look—for instance, do you ever find yourself acting on impulse, or experiencing sudden shifts in how you feel about yourself and the people close to you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep making lists of everything that happens—even the arguments—because if I don’t write them down they just swirl around and I feel like the house is falling apart. At the same time, when I’m obsessively arranging the shelves and cataloguing his stuff, I notice I miss his laugh and it feels like I’m pushing him away. I know I’m difficult, and I’m terrified that if I let a dish sit out or stop counting the days he’s late, everything will just collapse. Still, I can’t shake the feeling that if I keep everything in order, at least something will stay right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself double-checking your coworkers or tracking things like your partner being late, what goes through your mind about their motives and how much you can truly rely on them?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about the little things—like how many minutes he’s late, whether I logged it, whether the shelf stays exactly where I put it—because if I miss one detail everything feels like it could fall apart. At work I’m praised, but I can’t shake the feeling that if I don’t catch a typo or a mistake the whole case will collapse, and that same fear follows me home when he texts late at night. I want everything to be in order, but sometimes I wonder if anyone even notices when I’m not there, and that thought just makes me more rigid about keeping everything perfect.
